summary: Describes using the Camellia block cipher in Cipher Block Chaining mode, with an explicit initialization vector, for confidentiality in IPsec ESP. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Camellia is another way to scramble data with a key. This memo shows how to use it inside IPsec to keep messages private.

questions: what key sizes does camellia support
how does camellia work in ipsec esp
what is camellia cbc iana identifier
subtitle: How to use the Camellia block cipher in CBC mode to keep IPsec ESP packets confidential.

tldr.problem: IPsec ESP needs encryption algorithms to keep packet contents private, and Camellia, a cipher with the same interface as AES, had no definition for use there.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies Camellia in Cipher Block Chaining mode with a random explicit IV carried in every packet, 128-bit blocks, and 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys, plus the IANA identifiers that IKE uses to negotiate it.
tldr.outcome: Camellia becomes a standards-track confidentiality option for ESP, alongside the other ciphers ESP can use. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 4312 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 4303 (ESP) and RFC 3713 (the Camellia algorithm).

sections.title: Why Camellia in IPsec
sections.content:
RFC 4312 describes the use of the Camellia block cipher in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode, with an explicit Initialization Vector, as a confidentiality mechanism inside the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP).

The RFC says Camellia was selected as a recommended primitive by the EU NESSIE project and included in the list of cryptographic techniques for Japanese e-Government systems selected by CRYPTREC. It supports a 128-bit block size and 128-, 192- and 256-bit key lengths, the same interface as the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). It is a symmetric cipher with a Feistel structure, developed jointly by NTT and Mitsubishi Electric Corporation in 2000.

The document uses the RFC 2119 keywords (MUST, SHOULD, MAY) to say what an implementation has to do.
sections.plainLanguage: Camellia is a lock that works just like another famous lock called AES. This memo says how to use it on IPsec, the system that protects Internet messages.

sections.title: Camellia Characteristics
sections.content:
The RFC walks through the usual properties of a block cipher. For mode, it picks CBC, calling it well defined and well understood, and noting it is currently required for all other ESP ciphers. CBC needs an IV the same size as the block. The IV is XORed with the first plaintext block before encryption, and each later plaintext block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block.

Camellia supports three key sizes: 128, 192 and 256 bits. The default is 128 bits, and all implementations MUST support it. Supporting 192 and 256 bits is optional (MAY). The number of rounds depends on the key size, and implementations MUST use it.

The RFC states that at the time of writing there were no known weak keys for Camellia. For performance it only points to the Camellia web site and to NESSIE's independent report, and gives no numbers of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: Camellia scrambles data in chunks, and each chunk is mixed with the scrambled chunk before it. Everyone must support the standard key size, and bigger keys are optional extras.

sections.title: Key Sizes and Rounds
sections.content:
Key length decides how many rounds of scrambling the cipher performs. The RFC uses MUST for each pairing.

  • 128-bit key: 18 rounds (mandatory to support)
  • 192-bit key: 24 rounds (optional)
  • 256-bit key: 24 rounds (optional)

For the keying material, the amount of key bits handed from the key exchange protocol to ESP must be at least the key size. The encryption and decryption key is taken from the first 128, 192 or 256 bits of that material.
sections.plainLanguage: A longer secret key makes the scrambling go around more times. The shortest key is the one every device must know how to use.

sections.title: ESP Payload Layout and Padding
sections.content:
The ESP payload is the IV followed by the raw ciphertext. The IV is 16 octets, the same as the block size, and the encrypted payload that follows is variable in length but always a multiple of 16 octets.

The IV MUST be chosen at random and MUST be unpredictable. Implementations MUST NOT use a counter or other low Hamming-distance source for IVs, so that very similar plaintext blocks in different packets are not encrypted in a similar way. A random IV also prevents identical ciphertext from packets whose data is identical across the first block.

Because the IV travels in every datagram, each received datagram can be decrypted even when some datagrams are dropped or re-ordered in transit.

Padding MUST be added, as specified in the ESP document, so that the data to be encrypted (including the ESP Pad Length and Next Header fields) is a multiple of 16 octets. That also keeps those two fields right-aligned in a 4-octet word, so no extra padding is needed for a 4-octet boundary. Extra padding MAY be added as long as the 16-octet block size is kept.

The RFC notes no known issues between Camellia and other parts of ESP, such as the authentication schemes used with it.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet carries its own random starting number so it can be unlocked on its own, even if its neighbors go missing. The data is padded out so it fits neatly into 16-byte boxes.

sections.title: Negotiating Camellia with IKE
sections.content:
Camellia follows the same API as AES, so the RFC defines only two identifiers for the Internet Key Exchange (IKE). Anything else about how IKE interacts with the cipher is the same as for AES, which the RFC leaves to the AES-CBC document, RFC 3602.

  • Phase 1: Encryption Algorithm ID 8, for CAMELLIA-CBC.
  • Phase 2: ESP Transform Identifier 22, for ESP_CAMELLIA.

IANA has assigned both values.
sections.plainLanguage: Before two computers talk secretly, they agree on which code to use. These two numbers are how they say "let's use Camellia."

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations are encouraged to use the largest key sizes they can, weighing performance on their particular hardware and software. Encryption affects both ends of a secure channel, so the cost on the server side counts as well as the client side. Even so, the RFC says a key size of 128 bits is considered secure for the foreseeable future.

It also reports that no security problem has been found on Camellia, citing CRYPTREC and NESSIE.
sections.plainLanguage: Bigger keys are safer but slower, and both sides of the conversation pay the cost. The standard size is thought to be safe for a long time.
